knowledge_point.title: Evaluating the Line Integral of a Function Over Curve Expressed as a Function of Y

question.:question/problem:
![](/tmp/ca9837-templates-5ek4tgt5/17592186179718/curve-85e07c94540df01bb38ccb0d.png)

Evaluate the line integral
$$
\int_C 6 y\,\mathrm{d}s
$$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=2 y - 4$ between $(14,9)$ and $(8,6)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Set $y=t$. The endpoint $y$-coordinates give $6\le t\le 9$. Thus
$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r(t)&=\langle 2 t - 4,t\rangle \\ \mathbf r'(t)&=\langle 2,1\rangle \\ \|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{(2)^2+1}=\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$
Substitute both coordinates into the scalar function:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf r(t))&=6 t=6 t\end{aligned}
$$
Multiply by the arc-length factor:
$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C 6 y\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{6}^{9}\left(6 t\right)\left(\sqrt{5}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\int_{6}^{9}6 \sqrt{5} t\,\mathrm{d}t\end{aligned}
$$
Use the power rule and subtract the endpoint values:
$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C 6 y\,\mathrm{d}s&=\left[3 \sqrt{5} t^{2}\right]_{6}^{9} \\ &=\left(243 \sqrt{5}\right)-\left(108 \sqrt{5}\right) \\ &=135 \sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral
$$
\int_C 3 x^{6} e^{- 2 y}\,\mathrm{d}s
$$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=e^{\frac{y}{2}}$ between $(\sqrt{2},\ln{\left(2 \right)})$ and $(\sqrt{3},\ln{\left(3 \right)})$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Set $y=t$. The endpoint $y$-coordinates give $\ln{\left(2 \right)}\le t\le \ln{\left(3 \right)}$. Thus
$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r(t)&=\langle e^{\frac{t}{2}},t\rangle \\ \mathbf r'(t)&=\langle \frac{e^{\frac{t}{2}}}{2},1\rangle \\ \|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{\left(\frac{e^{\frac{t}{2}}}{2}\right)^2+1}=\frac{\sqrt{e^{t} + 4}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$
Substitute both coordinates into the scalar function:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf r(t))&=3 \left(e^{\frac{t}{2}}\right)^{6} e^{- 2 t}=3 e^{t}\end{aligned}
$$
Here $(e^{t/2})^6e^{-4t/2}=e^{(6-4)t/2}=e^{2t/2}$ by the exponent laws.

Multiply by the arc-length factor:
$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C 3 x^{6} e^{- 2 y}\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}^{\ln{\left(3 \right)}}\left(3 e^{t}\right)\left(\frac{\sqrt{e^{t} + 4}}{2}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\int_{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}^{\ln{\left(3 \right)}}\frac{3 \sqrt{e^{t} + 4} e^{t}}{2}\,\mathrm{d}t\end{aligned}
$$
Use $u=e^{t} + 4$, so $\mathrm{d}u=e^{t}\,\mathrm{d}t$; the new bounds are $6$ and $7$.
$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C 3 x^{6} e^{- 2 y}\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{6}^{7}\frac{3 \sqrt{u}}{2}\,\mathrm{d}u \\ &=\left[u^{\frac{3}{2}}\right]_{6}^{7} \\ &=\left(7 \sqrt{7}\right)-\left(6 \sqrt{6}\right) \\ &=- 6 \sqrt{6} + 7 \sqrt{7}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral
$$
\int_C \frac{6 x}{y}\,\mathrm{d}s
$$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $y^2=6x$ between $(\frac{20}{3},2 \sqrt{10})$ and $(\frac{8}{3},4)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First solve the curve equation for $x$: $y^2=6x$, so $x=\frac{y^{2}}{6}$.

Set $y=t$. The endpoint $y$-coordinates give $4\le t\le 2 \sqrt{10}$. Thus
$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r(t)&=\langle \frac{t^{2}}{6},t\rangle \\ \mathbf r'(t)&=\langle \frac{t}{3},1\rangle \\ \|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{\left(\frac{t}{3}\right)^2+1}=\frac{\sqrt{t^{2} + 9}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$
Substitute both coordinates into the scalar function:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf r(t))&=\frac{6 \left(\frac{t^{2}}{6}\right)}{t}=t\end{aligned}
$$
Multiply by the arc-length factor:
$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C \frac{6 x}{y}\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{4}^{2 \sqrt{10}}\left(t\right)\left(\frac{\sqrt{t^{2} + 9}}{3}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\int_{4}^{2 \sqrt{10}}\frac{t \sqrt{t^{2} + 9}}{3}\,\mathrm{d}t\end{aligned}
$$
Use $u=t^{2} + 9$, so $\mathrm{d}u=2 t\,\mathrm{d}t$; the new bounds are $25$ and $49$.
$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C \frac{6 x}{y}\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{25}^{49}\frac{\sqrt{u}}{6}\,\mathrm{d}u \\ &=\left[\frac{u^{\frac{3}{2}}}{9}\right]_{25}^{49} \\ &=\left(\frac{343}{9}\right)-\left(\frac{125}{9}\right) \\ &=\frac{218}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](/tmp/ca9837-templates-5ek4tgt5/17592186179718/curve-006e5ca88befd14ac9040832.png)

Evaluate the line integral
$$
\int_C 6 x y\,\mathrm{d}s
$$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=\sqrt{y}$ between $(2,4)$ and $(1,1)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Set $y=t$. The endpoint $y$-coordinates give $1\le t\le 4$. Thus
$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r(t)&=\langle \sqrt{t},t\rangle \\ \mathbf r'(t)&=\langle \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{t}},1\rangle \\ \|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{t}}\right)^2+1}=\frac{\sqrt{4 t + 1}}{2 \sqrt{t}}\end{aligned}
$$
Substitute both coordinates into the scalar function:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf r(t))&=6 \left(\sqrt{t}\right) t=6 t^{\frac{3}{2}}\end{aligned}
$$
Multiply by the arc-length factor:
$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C 6 x y\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{1}^{4}\left(6 t^{\frac{3}{2}}\right)\left(\frac{\sqrt{4 t + 1}}{2 \sqrt{t}}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\int_{1}^{4}3 t \sqrt{4 t + 1}\,\mathrm{d}t\end{aligned}
$$
Use $u=4 t + 1$, so $\mathrm{d}u=4\,\mathrm{d}t$; the new bounds are $5$ and $17$.
Also $t=(u-1)/4$, so the transformed integrand has two powers of $u$.
$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C 6 x y\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{5}^{17}\sqrt{u} \left(\frac{3 u}{16} - \frac{3}{16}\right)\,\mathrm{d}u \\ &=\left[\frac{3 u^{\frac{5}{2}}}{40} - \frac{u^{\frac{3}{2}}}{8}\right]_{5}^{17} \\ &=\left(\frac{391 \sqrt{17}}{20}\right)-\left(\frac{5 \sqrt{5}}{4}\right) \\ &=- \frac{5 \sqrt{5}}{4} + \frac{391 \sqrt{17}}{20}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](/tmp/ca9837-templates-5ek4tgt5/17592186179718/curve-369040660244e8183cc50605.png)

Evaluate the line integral
$$
\int_C \frac{6}{- x + y}\,\mathrm{d}s
$$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=2 y - 5$ between $(3,4)$ and $(-1,2)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Set $y=t$. The endpoint $y$-coordinates give $2\le t\le 4$. Thus
$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r(t)&=\langle 2 t - 5,t\rangle \\ \mathbf r'(t)&=\langle 2,1\rangle \\ \|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{(2)^2+1}=\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$
Substitute both coordinates into the scalar function:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf r(t))&=\frac{6}{- \left(2 t - 5\right) + t}=- \frac{6}{t - 5}\end{aligned}
$$
Multiply by the arc-length factor:
$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C \frac{6}{- x + y}\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{2}^{4}\left(- \frac{6}{t - 5}\right)\left(\sqrt{5}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\int_{2}^{4}- \frac{6 \sqrt{5}}{t - 5}\,\mathrm{d}t\end{aligned}
$$
Use $u=5 - t$, so $\mathrm{d}u=-1\,\mathrm{d}t$; the new bounds are $3$ and $1$.
$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C \frac{6}{- x + y}\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{3}^{1}- \frac{6 \sqrt{5}}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u \\ &=\left[- 6 \sqrt{5} \ln{\left(u \right)}\right]_{3}^{1} \\ &=\left(0\right)-\left(- 6 \sqrt{5} \ln{\left(3 \right)}\right) \\ &=6 \sqrt{5} \ln{\left(3 \right)}\end{aligned}
$$
Both logarithm arguments are positive. The identity $\ln A-\ln B=\ln(A/B)$ combines the endpoint logarithms.

question.:question/problem:
![](/tmp/ca9837-templates-5ek4tgt5/17592186179718/curve-cac18e15e65281a226e8ae57.png)

Evaluate the line integral
$$
\int_C 6 y^{3} e^{- x}\,\mathrm{d}s
$$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=\ln{\left(y \right)}$ between $(\ln{\left(2 \right)} + \frac{\ln{\left(6 \right)}}{2},2 \sqrt{6})$ and $(0,1)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Set $y=t$. The endpoint $y$-coordinates give $1\le t\le 2 \sqrt{6}$. Thus
$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r(t)&=\langle \ln{\left(t \right)},t\rangle \\ \mathbf r'(t)&=\langle \frac{1}{t},1\rangle \\ \|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{t}\right)^2+1}=\frac{\sqrt{t^{2} + 1}}{t}\end{aligned}
$$
Since $t>0$, the denominator in the norm simplifies without changing sign.

Substitute both coordinates into the scalar function:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf r(t))&=6 t^{3} e^{- \left(\ln{\left(t \right)}\right)}=6 t^{2}\end{aligned}
$$
Here $e^{-\ln t}=1/t$ because $t>0$.

Multiply by the arc-length factor:
$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C 6 y^{3} e^{- x}\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{1}^{2 \sqrt{6}}\left(6 t^{2}\right)\left(\frac{\sqrt{t^{2} + 1}}{t}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\int_{1}^{2 \sqrt{6}}6 t \sqrt{t^{2} + 1}\,\mathrm{d}t\end{aligned}
$$
Use $u=t^{2} + 1$, so $\mathrm{d}u=2 t\,\mathrm{d}t$; the new bounds are $2$ and $25$.
$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C 6 y^{3} e^{- x}\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{2}^{25}3 \sqrt{u}\,\mathrm{d}u \\ &=\left[2 u^{\frac{3}{2}}\right]_{2}^{25} \\ &=\left(250\right)-\left(4 \sqrt{2}\right) \\ &=250 - 4 \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](/tmp/ca9837-templates-5ek4tgt5/17592186179718/curve-eeff12dd42fe564b1a947d91.png)

Evaluate the line integral
$$
\int_C \frac{6 x}{y}\,\mathrm{d}s
$$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=y^{2}$ between $(20,2 \sqrt{5})$ and $(1,1)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Set $y=t$. The endpoint $y$-coordinates give $1\le t\le 2 \sqrt{5}$. Thus
$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r(t)&=\langle t^{2},t\rangle \\ \mathbf r'(t)&=\langle 2 t,1\rangle \\ \|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{(2 t)^2+1}=\sqrt{4 t^{2} + 1}\end{aligned}
$$
Substitute both coordinates into the scalar function:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf r(t))&=\frac{6 \left(t^{2}\right)}{t}=6 t\end{aligned}
$$
Multiply by the arc-length factor:
$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C \frac{6 x}{y}\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{1}^{2 \sqrt{5}}\left(6 t\right)\left(\sqrt{4 t^{2} + 1}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\int_{1}^{2 \sqrt{5}}6 t \sqrt{4 t^{2} + 1}\,\mathrm{d}t\end{aligned}
$$
Use $u=4 t^{2} + 1$, so $\mathrm{d}u=8 t\,\mathrm{d}t$; the new bounds are $5$ and $81$.
$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C \frac{6 x}{y}\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{5}^{81}\frac{3 \sqrt{u}}{4}\,\mathrm{d}u \\ &=\left[\frac{u^{\frac{3}{2}}}{2}\right]_{5}^{81} \\ &=\left(\frac{729}{2}\right)-\left(\frac{5 \sqrt{5}}{2}\right) \\ &=\frac{729}{2} - \frac{5 \sqrt{5}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](/tmp/ca9837-templates-5ek4tgt5/17592186179718/curve-0460e2df0bbfd3ae13d4d389.png)

Evaluate the line integral
$$
\int_C 6 x y^{6}\,\mathrm{d}s
$$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=\frac{2}{y}$ between $(\frac{1}{2},4)$ and $(1,2)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Set $y=t$. The endpoint $y$-coordinates give $2\le t\le 4$. Thus
$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r(t)&=\langle \frac{2}{t},t\rangle \\ \mathbf r'(t)&=\langle - \frac{2}{t^{2}},1\rangle \\ \|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{\left(- \frac{2}{t^{2}}\right)^2+1}=\frac{\sqrt{t^{4} + 4}}{t^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$
Since $t>0$, the denominator in the norm simplifies without changing sign.

Substitute both coordinates into the scalar function:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf r(t))&=6 \left(\frac{2}{t}\right) t^{6}=12 t^{5}\end{aligned}
$$
Multiply by the arc-length factor:
$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C 6 x y^{6}\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{2}^{4}\left(12 t^{5}\right)\left(\frac{\sqrt{t^{4} + 4}}{t^{2}}\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &=\int_{2}^{4}12 t^{3} \sqrt{t^{4} + 4}\,\mathrm{d}t\end{aligned}
$$
Use $u=t^{4} + 4$, so $\mathrm{d}u=4 t^{3}\,\mathrm{d}t$; the new bounds are $20$ and $260$.
$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C 6 x y^{6}\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{20}^{260}3 \sqrt{u}\,\mathrm{d}u \\ &=\left[2 u^{\frac{3}{2}}\right]_{20}^{260} \\ &=\left(1040 \sqrt{65}\right)-\left(80 \sqrt{5}\right) \\ &=- 80 \sqrt{5} + 1040 \sqrt{65}\end{aligned}
$$
